transcript.text: My Dyson V10 Absolute (SV12) won't run at all now. On the battery display there's a red light flashing when I press the trigger, then nothing. It was charging overnight. Do I need a new battery or is the whole thing dead?

Probably not the whole machine. A cordless that won't run but still lights up a battery warning when you press the trigger usually has a battery or charging problem, not a dead motor. I can't confirm exactly what that flashing red light means on your V10, so I'm working from the symptoms rather than treating it as a known code. The likely causes, most likely first:
• The battery never actually charged overnight: a charger, socket or charging-contact problem.
• The battery is worn out or has failed, so it won't hold or deliver a charge. This is very common on older V10s.
• The machine's protection is stopping it because of a blockage, a clogged filter, or the battery being too cold or too warm.
• Less likely: the trigger, motor or electronics inside, which you only consider once the others are ruled out. These checks will help tell them apart:
1. Plug the charger into a socket you know works and push the lead fully into the vacuum (or seat it properly on the dock). Wipe the charging contacts clean and dry first. If the battery lights come on and show it charging, the charger is working. If nothing lights up at all, the charger, socket or contacts are the likely problem rather than the battery.
2. Make sure it's charging somewhere at normal room temperature, not a cold garage or next to a radiator. Batteries often refuse to charge or run when they're too cold or hot. Then give it a full charge (around 3½ to 4 hours) and try again.
3. With the battery not in use, empty the bin and check the filter. If it's clogged, wash it in cold water and leave it to dry fully for 24 hours. Also look through the wand, the floorhead and the bin inlet for a blockage. If clearing something gets it running, it was protection cutting in, not a fault. If the charger lights up and shows charging but it still flashes red and won't run after a full charge, the battery is the most likely culprit. That's usually a far cheaper fix than replacing the vacuum. To start with: when you put it on charge, do the battery lights come on to show it's charging, or does nothing light up?

Yes, the blue lights come on when it's on the charger, though it sometimes then shows the flashing red too. I've tried a different socket and the charger light is on there as well. The battery isn't swollen, hot or smelly, if that matters.

That helps a lot. Blue lights on the charger at two different sockets means the charger and supply are doing their job, so we can largely rule them out. The telling part is the red flashing that sometimes appears while it's sitting on charge. It points much more towards the battery itself: either the cells or the battery's own management electronics have a fault, or it's refusing to charge because it's outside its comfortable temperature range. Not being swollen, hot or smelly is good news for safety, but a battery can fail without any of those signs. This is the strongest fit, especially if the machine is a few years old.
• Battery protection is stopping it because it's too cold or warm, or because of a blocked airway or clogged filter.
• Much less likely: the trigger, motor or main electronics. 1. Bring it into a normal room-temperature spot, not a garage, a cold windowsill or next to a radiator. Leave it an hour to settle, then charge it for a full 3½ to 4 hours without unplugging. If it then runs normally, temperature was the cause, not a fault. If it still flashes red while charging, that is a strong battery-fault sign.
2. If you haven't already, make sure the filter is clean and completely dry and nothing is stuck in the bin inlet, wand or floorhead. Only do this with it off the charger. If it then runs, it was protection. If not, it's the battery. If it still flashes red and won't run after both checks, the battery is very probably the culprit. A battery is usually a far cheaper fix than a new vacuum, and on the V10 it's a straightforward owner swap. Before spending anything, though, it's worth contacting Dyson support. They can talk you through their own battery diagnostics and confirm it, and depending on the machine's age and whether it was registered, it may still be under guarantee. If a known-good battery still won't make it run, that would point to the trigger or electronics inside, and at that point a repairer is the better route.
[Helpful to see: image "Poor suction — what to check first" — A vacuum that pulses or cuts out after running is usually a full bin, a dirty filter or a blockage starving the airflow — check and clear those before suspecting battery, charger or motor. Switch off and unplug first. Typical layout — your model may differ.]

I've already done those. It lives in the utility room at normal temperature, I charged it for over 3.5 hours straight from the charger, and the filter was washed last month with the bin empty and no blockages. It still flashes red when I press the trigger. It's about 4.5 years old with the original battery, so out of guarantee. I'd rather speak to Dyson about cost before I unscrew anything, so is it definitely the battery?

[Heading: Likely cause: battery — flat or failed (cordless)]
Not 100% definite, but it's very probably the battery. I'd put it well ahead of anything else. Here's why. What's left is a machine that flashes red when you press the trigger, and sometimes even while it's on charge. That pattern fits a battery that can no longer deliver power, or whose own protection circuit has shut it down. At 4.5 years on the original battery, that's about the age these batteries typically wear out. The only realistic alternative is a fault in the trigger switch or the main electronics. 1. If a known-good battery makes it run normally, the old battery was the fault. Job done.
2. If a known-good battery still gives the red flash and won't run, the fault is in the machine itself. At that point a Dyson repair or an independent repairer is the better route. Speaking to Dyson first is a sensible plan. • Ask them to run through their battery diagnostics with you. They can often confirm the fault over the phone from the light pattern.
• Ask for the cost of a genuine replacement battery, and whether they offer a repair service, so you can compare the two.
• I can't confirm which battery fits your exact machine, so give them the model and serial number from the label on the machine. Then they can supply the right one. If you buy elsewhere, stick to a genuine or reputable battery. Very cheap unbranded lithium packs are a common source of poor fit, short life and, occasionally, safety problems.
